display_title: Official Review of Paper1726 by Reviewer m3Ac

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a method to prune neurons of 2-layer multi-layer-perceptron for classification using a single pass over the training data.
The method scores each neuron of the single hidden layer according to a first-order approximation of the loss and removes the neurons with the lowest score.

The method is tested on MNIST and CIFAR-10 and compared to various baselines. An extension to deeper MLPs that involves combining the proposed method with existing baseline methods is briefly discussed.
content.main_review:
The authors describe the method as gradient-free, although it uses a pass over the training set where updates a mask according to a first-order approximation of the loss, which is similar to computing a gradient. There is no discussion of the pros and cons of "gradient-free" vs gradient-based methods.

All experiments use very simple network architectures on only two old, small and easy datasets (MNIST and CIFAR-10), so it's not clear how they generalize to more realistic datasets and network architectures.
The experiments involving fine-tuning show no differences for a 2-layer MLP and slight improvements for deeper networks.

Overall, I don't find the motivation compelling and the results convincing.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I don't find the motivation compelling and the results convincing.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1726 by Reviewer m3Ac

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
- “...which is similar to computing a gradient.” We are not able to see the similarities between OSSuM and gradient computation. OSSuM only requires the computation of neuron activations once for each data point (one forward propagation), while gradient methods do optimizations iteratively using multiple forward and backward propagations. Also, Figure 1 shows a comparison of OSSuM and gradient-based supermasks. OSSuM and its variants outperform the gradient-based supermasks at multiple settings. OSSuM does not require any hyperparameter tuning, while gradient-based supermasks require hyperparameter tuning for good performance.


- “All experiments use very simple network architectures... “As we discussed in section 5, we aim to extend OSSuM to deeper networks such as CNNs. We believe we are scratching the surface of some potential direction towards training neural networks much efficiently. At this stage, we feel it’s unfair to demand the application of OSSuM on larger architectures and datasets such as ImageNet.


- ‘The experiments involving fine-tuning show no differences for a 2-layer MLP and slight improvements for deeper networks.” In our work, we try to be more transparent by reporting all the relevant details about OSSuM experiments. We only observe “slight improvements” for deeper networks in experiments involving fine-tuning, but this could be an indication that the effect could amplify when OSSuM is scaled to larger datasets (which we leave for future work since it is out of scope of this paper). The objective of this experiment is to hint that OSSuM might be able to find winning lottery tickets at initialization. The major novelty of our paper is that OSSuM can be used to find a sparser network at **initialization** which gives a significantly higher classification accuracy than random chance **without any further training**. OSSuM achieves this in one-shot (not iterative optimization) and zero-gradient computation.


We believe we have answered all the queries and would appreciate a re-evaluation.

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
- “Does this apply to regression?” Like most of the prior works on pruning, OSSuM focuses on classification tasks.


- “How does Ossum compare to gradient-based fine-grain sparsification-at-initialization methods such as GraSP" It is unfair to compare GraSP with OSSuM since they are different algorithms designed for different purposes. GraSP uses gradient information to prune networks in an **unstructured** manner at **initialization**. This sparse network obtained at initialization has only accuracy similar to random chance (ie; $\sim$10% for MNIST). The sparse network requires further SGD training for achieving higher classification accuracy. OSSuM prunes neural networks in a **structured** manner (hence providing practical speedups on modern hardware) to obtain sparse networks with significantly higher accuracy ($\sim$82% on MNIST) at initialization without any SGD training.


- “The networks and datasets/tasks demonstrated (MLP on MNIST and CIFAR-10) are not representative of recent SoTA results, thusly of limited practical value.” As we discussed in section 5, we aim to extend OSSuM to deeper networks such as CNNs. We believe we are scratching the surface of some potential direction towards training neural networks much efficiently. At this stage, we feel it’s unfair to demand the application of OSSuM on larger architectures and datasets such as ImageNet.


We believe we have answered all the queries and would appreciate a re-evaluation.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1726 by Reviewer vc4j

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a neuron pruning method called One-Shot Supermasking (OSSuM). It aims at introducing the first gradient-free supermask at initialization.  The proposed method is evaluated on MNIST and CIFAR-10 using a fully-connected network.
content.main_review:
One of the main limitations of the proposed models lies in their evaluation. The paper could have been stronger if a better selection of benchmarking methods would have been used (e.g. Top KAST https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03517), such that the overall results to be at least comparable with state-of-the-art methods (preferable also on larger datasets, such as ImageNet-2012) in order to fully support the claims.  Some more related works to one-shot pruning at initialization should be considered and used to refine the claims (e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.02887).

As for the model itself, I think that it lacks a significant novelty. In the end, it is not fully clear to me how the supermask is generated? To what extend is the proposed method different in comparison with other sparse initializations (for example, the coreset-based pruning). It is also not clear why and how the implementation code of the coreset-based pruning method was used (as stated in the appendix).
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I think that the paper needs improvements in order to support the claims.

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
- “One of the main limitations of the proposed models lies in their evaluation… (e.g. Top KAST https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03517)... and used to refine the claims (e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.02887).” It is unfair to compare Top KAST or In-Time Overparametrization (or other prior works) and OSSuM. OSSuM prunes networks at **initialization** in **one-shot (and gradient-free)** to get a sparser network with significantly higher classification accuracy than random chance at initialization (OSSuM is the **very first algorithm** to do so). Top KAST and various other prior works iteratively prune (or dynamically prune) and train networks (**using gradients**) to obtain trained sparse networks. These methods are not designed to obtain accurate sparse networks at initialization.


- As we discuss in section 5, we aim to extend OSSuM to deeper networks such as CNNs. We believe we are scratching the surface of some potential direction towards training neural networks much efficiently. At this stage, we feel it’s unfair to demand the application of OSSuM on larger architectures and datasets such as ImageNet.


- “As for the model itself, I think that it lacks a significant novelty.” Algorithm 1 with scoring in equation (3) is used for generating the supermasks. Bottom $\Delta$ neurons (after ranking neurons based on scoring in equation (3)) get a binary mask value of 0 while the remaining neurons get a binary mask value of 1.  We believe that OSSuM is very novel. It is the first algorithm that can prune neural networks at initialization to obtain sparser networks with a significantly higher classification accuracy than random chance (eg; 82% on MNIST at initialization). OSSuM efficiently (one-shot and gradient-free) and approximately (using greedy algorithms) finds the solution to the NP-hard supermasking problem discussed in [1].


- “To what extend is the proposed method different in comparison with other sparse initializations (for example, the coreset-based pruning).” Coreset-based pruning is **not** a method for computing sparse initializations. Coreset-based methods and most of the prior works focus on pruning fully trained neural networks. OSSuM prunes networks at initialization and has a significantly higher classification accuracy than random chance. OSSuM is the very **first algorithm** to do so.


- “It is also not clear why and how the implementation code of the coreset-based pruning method was used (as stated in the appendix).” Coreset-based pruning (as discussed in section 4.1) is used as a baseline for experiments where pruning is performed on fully trained networks (**not** at initialization). “Coreset” curves in Figure 2 refer to the coreset-based pruning by Mussay et al. At higher sparsities, OSSuM has a clear advantage over coreset-based pruning while pruning fully trained neural networks. Coreset-based pruning **can not** (while OSSuM can) prune neural networks at initializations to obtain a neural network with significantly higher classification accuracy than random chance.


We believe we have answered all the queries and would appreciate a re-evaluation.


[1] Eran Malach, Gilad Yehudai, Shai Shalev-Schwartz, and Ohad Shamir. Proving the lottery ticket hypothesis: Pruning is all you need. In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 6682– 6691. PMLR, 2020

display_title: Official Review of Paper1726 by Reviewer gN1p

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposed an one-shot gradient-free pruning method to prune randomly initialized neural networks. 
Starting from a theory on two-layer MLP, the method is derived and then extended to multi-layer MLP. 
The authors evaluate their method and variants under different settings including `Pruning at initialization` and `Pruning after training`.
content.main_review:
* The authors claim that their method is designed to prune a randomly initialized neural network. In addition, **the ultimate goal** is to make sure that training the pruned neural network will eventually get a similar accuracy as training a dense one. However, during the author deriving their theory, their object function (equ.1) is **to minimize the cross-entropy loss after pruning at initialization**. I didn't follow why/how is equ.1 related to the **ultimate goal**. 

* `For deeper networks, we use a combination of OSSuM + Norm based pruning — the initial layers being pruned using norm of the neurons, followed by the use of OSSuM in the last layer.' I am not sure about what is the norm of neuron. Did the authors mean the norm of neuron's weights? If so, only the last layer is pruned with the proposed method. 

* All experiments are conducted on relatively simple architectures and small-scale datasets. Since the proposed method is a kind of greedy pruning method, I cannot expect how the proposed method perform on deeper convolution neural networks and larger datasets. 

* The comparison with APoZ [1] would be interesting. Both APoZ and OSSuM require a traversing of the training set and are gradient-free. 

[1] Hu, Hengyuan, et al. "Network trimming: A data-driven neuron pruning approach towards efficient deep architectures." arXiv preprint arXiv:1607.03250 (2016).
content.summary_of_the_review: Pruning neural network at initialization is an important task for efficient training. However, the novelty, rationality, and effectiveness require more improvements.

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
- “In addition, **the ultimate goal** is to make sure that training the pruned neural network will eventually get a similar accuracy as training a dense one.” We do not claim this in our paper. Our goal is to build a sparse neural network at initialization with one forward propagation that performs significantly better than random chance without any gradient-based iterative training (for example, % on MNIST with just one forward pass on data). Later the sparse networks can be trained (or used for inferencing) using gradient-based methods with significantly lesser memory and computations. Memory and computational benefits that OSSuM provides are practical since OSSuM performs structured pruning.


- “I didn't follow why/how is equ.1 related to the **ultimate goal**.”.  We do not claim that equation (1) is used for obtaining a fully trained sparse network with accuracy similar to the fully trained larger overparameterized network. However, equation (1) is used for obtaining a sparse neural network **at initialization** with significantly higher classification accuracy, which may later be trained using SGD for competitive accuracies. In our paper, we do pruning in one-shot (and gradient-free) to obtain a network with 82% accuracy on MNIST **at initialization**. This is the novelty of our work.


- “I am not sure about what is the norm of neuron.” Norm of the neuron refers to the L2 norm of the weight associated with the neuron. We make this clear in baselines (4.1) and later sections with appropriate references.


 - “I cannot expect how the proposed method perform on deeper convolution neural networks and larger datasets.” Our work is the first practical algorithm that performs pruning **at initialization** to provide a sparser network with significantly higher classification accuracy than random chance. In fact, we approximately solve the NP-hard problem in [1] in **one-shot** and **gradient-free**. As we discussed in section 5, we aim to extend OSSuM to deeper networks such as CNNs. We believe we are scratching the surface of some potential direction towards training neural networks much efficiently by achieving highly accurate networks at initialization. At this stage, we feel it’s unfair to demand the application of OSSuM on larger datasets and architectures.


- “Both APoZ and OSSuM require a traversing of the training set and are gradient-free.” It is very unfair to compare APoZ and OSSuM. OSSuM prunes networks at **initialization** in **one-shot (and gradient-free)** to get a sparser network with significantly higher classification accuracy than random chance at initialization (OSSuM is the very first algorithm to do so). APoZ and various other prior works **iteratively** prune and retrain networks (**using gradients**) to obtain trained sparse networks. 


We believe we have answered all the queries and would appreciate a re-evaluation.


[1] Eran Malach, Gilad Yehudai, Shai Shalev-Schwartz, and Ohad Shamir. Proving the lottery ticket hypothesis: Pruning is all you need. International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 6682– 6691. PMLR, 2020

display_title: A common reply to all the reviewers

content.title: A common reply to all the reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their comments. We first provide a common reply to the reviewers to clarify some common questions. Subsequently, each reviewer’s comments are addressed separately.

- In this paper, the aim is **not to** prune a neural network to maintain the same accuracy as the prior works. OSSuM is useful in pruning:

  - a **randomly initialized** network to get a subnetwork with significantly higher accuracy than random chance **without** any training (also known as supermasking). OSSuM is the **first practical algorithm** that approximately solves the NP-hard problem of supermasking, identified in [1], in **one-shot** with a theoretical backing. For example, OSSuM takes as input a randomly initialized network having 10% test accuracy on MNIST and prunes it to obtain a subnetwork (retaining the original weights) with 82% test accuracy **without any training with just one forward pass on the dataset** (Figure 1e). This is the major **novelty** of our work. Prior to our work, an efficient method of finding such a subnetwork was unknown.

  - a fully trained neural network to obtain a subnetwork with significantly higher accuracy than the baselines (norm-based and coreset-based pruning) at very high sparsity (dashed curves in Figure 2).


- Our work differs from the prior works such as SNIP [2], GraSP [3], and SynFlow [4] where they attempt to prune neural networks at initializations to obtain subnetworks that **require** further gradient training for achieving good test accuracy. These works are **not** designed to prune networks at initialization to obtain a subnetwork with higher classification accuracy. Hence, we do not compare OSSuM with these works.


- Our work differs from prior works such as [5,6,7] where they **iteratively** train the overparameterized networks with constant sparsity using gradients to obtain a fully trained network. These works are designed for sparse training of neural networks using **unstructured** sparsity. We do not compare OSSuM with [5,6,7] since OSSuM prunes neural networks at **initialization** to obtain sparse networks with higher classification accuracy without any gradient-based training.


- Motivations for OSSuM.

  - [1] proves the existence of subnetworks in sufficiently overparameterized networks that have high classification accuracy at **initialization without** any training. OSSuM is the **first practical algorithm** to approximately solve this problem in **one-shot** (with one forward pass over the dataset). This has very interesting theoretical motivations since we obtain good subnetworks in one-shot by only masking, without any gradient-based training.

  - Practically, OSSuM could be useful in scenarios where there is a small training budget for both computation and memory. A single random seed value can be used to store a full network at initialization. OSSuM finds the binary mask value for each neuron in the network in one-shot. Essentially for transmitting a given network architecture from one system to another, OSSuM requires storing just one seed value and a binary mask. For example, (based on Figure 1) OSSuM can store a 2-layer network with 1000 hidden neurons and **80% test accuracy** on MNIST using just **125 B** of memory (note that this network was computed with just one forward pass on the dataset at network initialization). A full network with the same architecture trained using SGD would require 5-10 forward and backward passes on the dataset and **$\sim$3 MB** to achieve $\sim$100% test accuracy. Here, OSSuM gives a **$\sim$15-30X** computation gain and **$\sim$25,000X** memory gain with a 20% drop in test accuracy when compared to the full network trained using SGD. Also, OSSuM **does not** require any hyperparameter tuning.

  - Yet another consequence of OSSuM is in a setup where we have a large training data on which only one pass is feasible (streaming model). OSSuM is able to guarantee  **80% accuracy** on such a setup (on MNIST), where the memory required is only proportional to the number of neurons in the initial network (in order to calculate activations). 


- In the future, we aim to extend OSSuM for deeper networks for evaluating OSSuM on larger networks (such as ResNets) and datasets (such as ImageNet). Considering OSSuM as one of the first steps towards supermasking, we believe that extending OSSuM to deeper networks is beyond the scope of this work.


We believe we have answered all the queries and would appreciate a re-evaluation.
